Lichen

/LY-kun/ — stress on first syllable, rhymes with 'chicken' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Lichen is a small, crusty or leaf-like organism, made of fungus and algae growing together, that spreads across rocks, trees, and other surfaces.

Pale green lichen crusted the north side of every boulder.

Worked Example

The ancient stone bridge was patched with lime-green and rust-colored lichen, a living map of centuries of weather.

The lichen here is the visible, crusty organism covering the stone — a partnership of fungus and algae working together. Lichen is more precise than 'growth' or 'coating' because it names the specific symbiotic pairing, not just any surface layer.

How Lichen Sits Among Its Neighbors

Antonyms

sterile

How Strong Is It? — crust → growth → organism → lichen

crust vs. lichen

crust vs. lichen: A crust is just a hard surface layer of anything, while a lichen is a specific living crust formed by a fungus and an alga growing together.

growth vs. lichen

growth vs. lichen: Growth is a vague word for anything that spreads over a surface, but a lichen is one particular kind of growth — a fungus-and-algae partnership on rock or bark.

organism vs. lichen

organism vs. lichen: Organism is the broadest term, meaning any living thing at all, whereas a lichen is a very specific organism made of two life forms living as one.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — lichen

Root — lichen: tree-moss; literally 'that which licks / eats around itself' (from Greek 'leichein', to lick) (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Lichen comes from a Greek word meaning 'to lick,' picturing the organism as something that 'licks' or eats its way across a surface — just as lichen slowly spreads over rocks and bark.

Use the root in a new word: lick

Use the root in a new word: lick: The everyday word 'lick' traces back to the same ancient root ('to lick') as lichen, which was named for the way it seems to lick its way slowly across rocks and tree bark.

Word Choice

neutral / scientific

Lichen is the precise term for this specific two-part organism, so use it when describing the fungus-algae partnership. When you just want to say 'something's growing on the rock' without specifying what, 'growth' or 'coating' works fine. Lichen shines in science contexts where the specific nature of the organism matters.
